concepts.title: Concept of Planning
concepts.definition: The managerial function of settling in advance both the targets to be pursued and the route to reach them, so that the distance between an organisation's present position and its desired one is crossed deliberately.
concepts.key_idea: Planning handles ends and means together: it fixes objectives for a period, drafts alternative courses of action, and picks the best among them.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs104.txt lines 90-159 (Concept; deciding in advance; ends and means)
question_patterns: what is meant by planning

solution_steps.explain: Planning means deciding in advance what is to be done and how it is to be done.

solution_steps.action: Bring in objectives and courses of action
solution_steps.explain: Targets are set for a period, alternative routes are drafted, and the most suitable route is chosen.
Planning carries the organisation from its current position toward the position it wants to occupy.

concepts.title: Importance of Planning
concepts.definition: The benefits the function delivers: it gives every unit a common direction, lowers the danger from uncertainty through forecasts, trims duplicated and useless work, turns fresh ideas into concrete plans, sharpens decision making, and supplies the yardsticks that controlling later measures against.
concepts.key_idea: Six benefits -- direction, less uncertainty, less overlapping, innovation, better decisions, standards for controlling; planning is the prerequisite of controlling.

solution_steps.action: Pick the benefit the question targets
solution_steps.explain: Recall the six standard benefits of planning.
For example, forecasts prepared during planning anticipate changes so that responses are ready in advance.

solution_steps.action: State the consequence of not planning
solution_steps.explain: Without plans, employees drift in different directions and deviations cannot even be detected.

concepts.title: Features of Planning
concepts.definition: Seven marks of the function: it exists to reach objectives, comes before every other managerial function, runs at all levels and departments, never stops, peers into the future through forecasting, demands a choice among alternatives, and stays an intellectual exercise rather than physical doing.
concepts.key_idea: Primacy means all other functions operate inside the frame the plan sets; pervasiveness means top plans the whole firm, middle plans departments, supervisors plan daily operations.

solution_steps.explain: For instance, planning being continuous means each plan is followed by another on fresh conditions.
Link the case detail explicitly to the named feature.

concepts.title: Limitations of Planning
concepts.definition: The drawbacks of the function: fixed plans can turn rigid when circumstances move, a shifting environment defeats forecasts, lower levels lose their creative voice, preparing plans costs heavy money and time, and even an old winning plan offers no promise of repeating its success.
concepts.key_idea: Six limitations -- rigidity, dynamic environment, reduced creativity, huge cost, time consumption, no guarantee of success.

solution_steps.explain: Match the case or statement to the standard list of six limitations.
For example, following a pre-decided plan after circumstances have changed can harm the organisation.
Planning is still worth doing -- a tool to use with caution, not a cure for every problem.

concepts.title: Steps in the Planning Process
concepts.definition: Seven ordered steps: fix the objectives, build the premises or assumptions about the future, list every possible course of action, weigh each against feasibility and consequence, choose the best one, put it into action, and monitor how it runs.
concepts.key_idea: The real decision point arrives at selecting an alternative; a sales manager drafting option lists is performing the identifying-alternatives step.

For instance, drafting options like new markets or more advertising is identifying alternative courses of action.
One or two lines on the work done at that step and why it matters.

concepts.title: Single-use versus Standing Plans
concepts.definition: Two families of operational plans: single-use plans serve one non-repeating event or project and cover budgets, programmes and projects, while standing plans handle activities that recur regularly and cover policies, procedures, methods and rules.
concepts.key_idea: The test is repetition -- a seminar next month needs a single-use plan; e-payment for all daily bills is a standing rule.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs104.txt lines 937-1009 (Single-use and standing plans, their contents)
question_patterns: distinguish between single use plans and standing plans

solution_steps.explain: One-time project points to a single-use plan; recurring activity points to a standing plan.
Single-use: budget, programme, project. Standing: policy, procedure, method, rule.
For example, a rule states exactly what must be done with no discretion, and applies every day.

concepts.title: Objectives and Strategy
concepts.definition: Objectives are the end results an organisation wants to reach, stated measurably and within a time limit; strategy is the comprehensive top-level plan that combines long-run objectives, the chosen course of action, and the allocation of resources needed, all read against the environment and competition.
concepts.key_idea: Strategy has three dimensions -- determine long-term objectives, adopt a course of action, allocate resources; objectives are the end points everything else serves.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs104.txt lines 1035-1136 (Objectives; Strategy and its three dimensions)
question_patterns: define objectives as a type of plan

solution_steps.explain: Objectives give the desired future position; strategy gives the comprehensive route.

solution_steps.action: List strategy's three dimensions when asked
solution_steps.explain: Long-term objectives, the course of action adopted, and the resources allocated.
A telecom firm doubling daily data on a prepaid plan against a rival illustrates a competitive strategy move.

concepts.title: Policy, Procedure, Method and Rule
concepts.definition: The ladder of standing plans: a policy is a general statement that channels thinking and leaves room for discretion, a procedure spells the chronological steps inside that policy, a method prescribes how one step of a procedure is performed, and a rule is a blunt specific command admitting no discretion at all.
concepts.key_idea: Discretion shrinks down the ladder -- widest under policy, narrow at procedure, technical at method, zero at rule.
question_patterns: differentiate between policy and procedure
why are rules considered to be plans

solution_steps.action: Place the plan on the ladder
solution_steps.explain: Policy guides thinking, procedure sequences the steps, method handles one step, rule commands exactly.
Policies invite interpretation; rules allow none -- that contrast answers most such questions.

solution_steps.action: Add one fresh example per type
solution_steps.explain: Pricing policy, requisition procedure, lecture method of training, reporting time rule.

concepts.title: Programme and Budget as Plans
concepts.definition: A programme is the detailed project statement that bundles objectives, policies, procedures, rules, tasks, resources and the money allotted, while a budget is a plan expressed purely in numbers so that actual figures can later be compared with expected ones and corrected.
concepts.key_idea: A budget quantifies a plan and doubles as a control device -- deviations of actual from budgeted figures stand out immediately.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs104.txt lines 1249-1295 (Programme; Budget as a numerical plan and control device)
question_patterns: what is a budget and why is it also called a control device
how does a programme differ from a budget in planning
which type of plan states expected results in numerical terms
a forecast of expected sales of different products each month is which type of plan
what details does a programme include for implementing a project

solution_steps.explain: Programme: the whole project bundle in detail. Budget: the plan in numbers.

solution_steps.action: Show the control role of a budget
solution_steps.explain: Because every item is quantified, actual results are set against expected ones and deviations invite corrective action.
A monthly product-wise sales forecast or a worker requirement at peak production are typical budgets.

concepts.title: Cash Budget -- Surplus or Deficiency
concepts.definition: A period statement of the cash a firm expects to collect and the cash it expects to pay; netting the two reveals whether the firm will sit on spare cash or fall short and need to arrange funds.
concepts.key_idea: Collections below payments mean a deficiency to finance; spare cash sitting idle earns almost nothing, so the firm sizes its cash need with care.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs104.txt lines 1296-1318 (cash budget: estimated inflows and outflows, surplus or deficiency)
question_patterns: a firm expects cash receipts of {cash_inflows} and cash payments of {cash_outflows} this quarter work out its closing cash surplus or deficiency

solution_steps.explain: Expected cash sales and similar receipts are listed for the period.
A positive figure is a surplus to deploy; a negative one is a deficiency that must be financed.

worked_examples.question: Using Cash Budget -- Surplus or Deficiency, compute the result for cash_inflows = 3, cash_outflows = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Take the collections estimate: receipts = cash_inflows = 3.0 Step 2: Net the payments off: net_cash_position = receipts - cash_outflows = 0.0 Final result: 0.0

worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Take the collections estimate: receipts = cash_inflows = 4.0 Step 2: Net the payments off: net_cash_position = receipts - cash_outflows = 0.0 Final result: 0.0
